title: Merge Without Asking

post.author: u/chapter_nine_nomvula
post.title: My co-writer and I share one manuscript across nine time zones. Today's read-through found a sentence in chapter 9 that neither of us wrote.

blocks.text: I'm Nomvula. I write thrillers by night in Johannesburg with Beckett, who writes by day in Tucson, Arizona. Neither place changes its clocks, so he is always nine hours behind me. Our fourth book, *The Only Key*, is due at our publisher on Friday.

For six years we have taken turns, with a handover note at the end of each shift. He writes 08:00 to 14:00 his time, which is 17:00 to 23:00 mine. I write 23:00 to 05:00. At 17:00 my time, his 08:00, we hold the morning read-through on a video call, reading the newest pages aloud.

Our writing app keeps a whole copy of the book on each laptop, so we can write offline, without the internet. Changes travel through the app's server, a computer at the app company that passes them between our laptops.

It never sends the whole text, only changes, and each says what and where: "at position 40, insert never". A position is a count of characters, meaning every letter, space and full stop, from the start of the paragraph. The first character is position 0.

Syncing goes in three steps. My laptop sends its new changes to the server. It fetches Beckett's. Then it replays each of his: it counts to that position in my copy and makes the change there. His laptop does the same with mine.

On Tuesday 2 March I flew home from a book festival in Cape Town. My laptop went offline when I boarded, at 20:15, and found our home Wi-Fi at 23:42. Deadline week, so I worked on the plane, early. At 21:26 my time, 12:26 his, Beckett was mid-shift. We were both in chapter 9, paragraph 3.

Below: that paragraph before the flight, then the app's history. Each change line shows the time (mine), the change's id, a label no other change has, like a parcel's tracking number, then whose laptop and the change. Last, both copies after my sync.

before  Rain again. Kaja heard it. The door was locked. She had the only key.
21:20   N-412  mine, offline   delete 12 characters at position 0
21:26   B-388  his, online     insert "never " at position 40
23:42   my laptop syncs: sends N-412, replays B-388 at position 40
mine    Kaja heard it. The door was locked. She never had the only key.
his     Kaja heard it. The door was never locked. She had the only key.
She never had the only key. Neither of us wrote that.

I didn't look that night; I wrote chapter 10 until 05:00. At Wednesday's read-through Beckett read his line aloud: "The door was never locked." On my screen the door was locked, and Kaja never had the only key. He thought I had planted a twist. I thought he had.

blocks.label: chapter9_night_of_2_march.png

diagram.aria: Four hours from 20:00 to 24:00 on Tuesday 2 March 2027, Johannesburg time, one row per laptop. My laptop is online from 20:00 to 20:15, offline from 20:15 to 23:42, on the plane and then the way home, then holds the wrong paragraph after its sync. Beckett's laptop is online all evening. Markers: 21:20 I delete 12 characters; 21:26 he inserts at position 40; 23:42 my laptop syncs and never lands 12 characters late.

blocks.caption: Redrawn from the app's history, Tuesday 2 March 2027, my time; Beckett's is 9 hours earlier. My laptop was offline from 20:15, when I boarded in Cape Town, until 23:42 at home; the plane landed at 22:50. Green is a laptop online with its paragraph right; red is my copy after the sync, with never 12 characters late. His copy stayed right.

blocks.text: "Rain again. " is 12 characters. Beckett counted 40 in a paragraph that still had them, just before "locked". My laptop counted 40 in my shortened copy: 12 characters later, just before "had". In six years of turns, the app never had to merge: fit two changes made at once into one paragraph.
The manuscript goes in on Friday, and the copy-edits come back in April, the week I fly to Durban. What should Beckett and I change before then?

comments.author: u/grey_pager
comments.text: A position is only a count, and a count means something only in the text it was counted in. Test that against your history before you choose. Which text was Beckett counting in at 21:26, and which was your laptop counting in at 23:42? His laptop replayed your delete as well: why did his copy come out right? And if your 21:20 change had been an insert of 12 characters at position 0 instead of a delete, where would his word have landed on your laptop?

replies.author: u/chapter_nine_nomvula
replies.text: He counted in the paragraph that still began with "Rain again." My laptop counted in the one without it. His copy came out right because my delete sat at position 0, in front of his word, and a change further along a paragraph never moves the count to an earlier spot. If I had inserted 12 characters instead, his word would have landed 12 characters early.

comments.author: u/last_save_mehtap
comments.text: Last save wins is how every sync tool works, and it would have spared you this. Each laptop sends its whole version of the paragraph, meaning the full text as that laptop has it. The server keeps whichever version reaches it last and sends that one to both laptops, so the copies always match: no stray words, nothing half done. The rest is on you two. Just stop editing offline.

replies.author: u/chapter_nine_nomvula
replies.text: Beckett likes copies that always match, but he would rather have a lock. Before either of us edits a chapter, the app would ask the server for that chapter's lock. Only one of us can hold it at a time; the other can read the chapter but not type in it until it is handed back.

comments.author: u/margin_notes_neftali
comments.text: Every change in your history already carries the time it was typed. Collect both laptops' changes, sort them by that time, and have each laptop replay them in that order on the paragraph you both last had. Same changes, same order, same paragraph on both screens. Google Docs does something fancier called operational transformation: every change goes through one server, which shifts its position past the changes it has already applied. Your app has no such thing, and you need a fix by April.

reply.prompt: The copy-edits come back in April, and Nomvula flies home from Durban on Tuesday 13 April. What should she and Beckett change before then? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Keep whichever version of the paragraph reaches the server last, so both copies match.
options.part2: Beckett switched the app to last save wins on Thursday 4 March, and the manuscript went in on Friday. In the sim, replaying 2 March: my paragraph reaches the server last, at 23:42, so both laptops read "Kaja heard it. The door was locked. She had the only key." They match, and his "never" is gone without a word. On Tuesday 13 April, copy-edits, I flew home from Durban offline from 20:30 and added "Then silence. " to the start of that paragraph at 21:10. At 21:31 my time, 12:31 his, Beckett added " Someone else had a key." to its end. My laptop reached the server at 23:05, last, and its paragraph replaced his. Nothing told either of us. At Wednesday's read-through he asked where his line had gone: 5 words, lost, and both laptops agreed it had never been there.
options.senior: Last save wins makes the copies match by throwing one writer's work away. It is fine for a value where only the newest matters, such as a phone number, but a paragraph two people edit apart holds both edits, and keeping one whole version drops the other whole edit, silently. Here the version that reached the server last won, which was simply whoever landed later; with stamps from each laptop's clock it would be Rule 6 as well. Match by merging both edits, not by choosing between them: pin inserts to ids, or transform them through one server.

options.text: Give each character its own id, and pin each insert to its neighbour, not a position.
options.part2: Beckett found a writing app built on Yjs, a CRDT: every character gets an id no other character has, and each insert is pinned to the id of the character before it. We moved the book on Monday 8 March, after the manuscript went in. In the sim, replaying 2 March with ids: "never " is pinned after N7240, the space before "locked"; my delete hides N7201 to N7212; and both laptops read "Kaja heard it. The door was never locked. She had the only key." On Tuesday 13 April I flew home from Durban offline and added "Then silence. " at the start at 21:10; at 21:31 he added " Someone else had a key." at the end. My laptop came back at 23:05 and both laptops merged without asking anyone: "Then silence. Kaja heard it. The door was never locked. She had the only key. Someone else had a key." At Wednesday's read-through we read the same words, and they were the words we meant.
options.senior: A position means something only in the text it was counted in, so any merge that replays raw positions breaks as soon as two edits are made apart. Give every character an id and record an insert as "after this id": the neighbour is still there in every copy, so the insert lands where it was meant whatever arrived first, and deletes hide ids rather than counting. Every copy applies the same rule, with a fixed tie rule for two inserts after one neighbour, so all copies end the same without asking anyone: a CRDT, as in Yjs or Automerge. The other sound route is operational transformation, as in Google Docs: every change goes through one server that shifts its position past changes already applied. Either way, overlapping edits still deserve a human read, because merging the same way everywhere is not the same as merging the way both writers meant.

options.text: Lock a chapter while one of you edits it, so two edits can never land on one spot.
options.verdict: Trade-off: safe, but nobody writes offline
options.part2: Beckett turned on the chapter lock on Thursday 4 March. In the sim, replaying 2 March: offline, my laptop can't take the lock, so my 21:20 delete is blocked; at 23:42 I take it and make the delete, and both laptops read "Kaja heard it. The door was never locked. She had the only key." On Tuesday 13 April I sat on the Durban flight with chapter 9 open and couldn't type a word in it. I wrote "Then silence." on my boarding pass and typed it in at 23:05. Nothing was lost. But the plane hours I used to write in are gone, and on deadline nights we can no longer both work in one chapter at once.
options.senior: A lock removes the problem by removing the overlap: only one writer can change a chapter at a time, so every change is made on the latest text and raw positions stay right. The price is everything overlap gave you. An offline laptop can't get the lock, so nobody writes on a plane or a train, and two people can't work in one chapter together. A lock also needs a way to be taken back from a laptop that dies holding it. It is a sound choice for a small team that rarely overlaps, and a poor one for a tool sold on working anywhere; ids pinned to neighbours keep the overlap and still merge correctly.

options.text: Sort both laptops' changes by the time each was typed, and replay them in that order.
options.part2: Beckett set the app to sort every change by the time it was typed and have both laptops replay them in that order. In the sim, replaying 2 March: my delete (21:20) goes first and his insert (21:26) second, still at position 40, so both laptops read "Kaja heard it. The door was locked. She never had the only key." They match now, and both are wrong. On Tuesday 13 April my "Then silence. " (21:10, offline) sorted before his " Someone else had a key." (21:31), which was still counted at position 63, and both laptops read "... She had Someone else had a key. the only key." His sentence sat 14 characters early. At Wednesday's read-through we read it aloud together, word for wrong word.
options.senior: Sorting gives every laptop the same order, so the copies match, but each change still carries a position counted in the text its writer had, and replaying it after a change the writer never saw puts it in the wrong place on every copy at once. Order was never the problem; the count was. And the times come from two laptops' clocks, which drift and can be set wrong: Rule 6, never trust the clock on the wall. A merge needs either positions shifted past changes the writer hadn't seen, as operational transformation does, or no positions at all, as ids pinned to neighbours do.

sim.title: Replay chapter 9 on both laptops
sim.lede: You're Nomvula ("my laptop" in the log), replaying Tuesday 2 March 2027 from 20:00, Johannesburg time, one step at a time. As given data: both laptops hold chapter 9, paragraph 3, "Rain again. Kaja heard it. The door was locked. She had the only key.", 69 characters, positions counted from 0. My laptop is offline from 20:15 to 23:42. At 21:20 I delete 12 characters at position 0 (change N-412); at 21:26 Beckett, online, inserts "never " at position 40 (B-388), just before "locked". Replay positions: each laptop makes the other's change at the position the change gives. Last save wins: each laptop sends its whole paragraph and the server keeps the one that reaches it last. Sort by time: both laptops replay every change, in the order typed, from the paragraph they last shared. Operational transformation: every change goes through the server, which shifts its position past changes it has already applied that its writer had not seen. CRDT (copies that always merge to the same result): every character has an id, N7201 to N7269 for the paragraph and B9301 on for his insert; an insert is pinned to the id before it, and a delete hides ids. Chapter lock: a laptop must take the lock from the server before typing. The second night, Tuesday 13 April, starts from the paragraph as both meant it: offline 20:30 to 23:05, at 21:10 I insert "Then silence. " at position 0, and at 21:31 he inserts " Someone else had a key." at position 63, the end.
sim.tryThis: Try this: play it as on the night: my laptop replays B-388 at position 40, "never" lands 12 late before "had", his copy is right, and the laptops don't match. Set my laptop online: he types at 28 and both match. Last save wins: both match, 1 word lost. Sort by time: both match, both 12 late. Operational transformation: the server sends B-388 to my laptop shifted from 40 to 28. CRDT: "never " pinned after N7240 lands right on both. Chapter lock: my delete is blocked until 23:42. Then 13 April: replayed positions put his sentence 14 early; last save wins loses 5 words; transformation and the CRDT both give the 101-character paragraph.

explain.oneLine: Nothing in the app broke its own rule. A position is a count, and Beckett's 40 was counted in a paragraph that still began "Rain again. "; Nomvula's laptop counted it in one that didn't, so "never" landed 12 characters late. Pin every insert to the id of the character beside it, or send every change through one server that shifts the count, and both laptops agree on where he meant.

steps.title: A position means something only in the text it was counted in.
steps.text: The app's sync goes in steps. First, a laptop sends its new changes to the server. Second, it fetches the other laptop's. Third, it replays each one: it counts to the position the change gives and makes it there. The change id only stops a change being applied twice; nothing checks what the count was counted in. Beckett typed "never " at position 40 of the 69-character paragraph, just before "locked". At 21:20, offline, Nomvula had deleted positions 0 to 11, so in her 57-character copy everything after the cut sat 12 places earlier: "locked" at 28, "had" at 40. At 23:42 her laptop replayed his insert at 40, 12 characters late, inside the next sentence. His laptop replayed her delete at position 0, in front of his word, and a change further along never moves the count to an earlier spot, so his copy came out right and the two laptops now held different paragraphs. Nothing warned either of them. It needs concurrent edits, made without either writer having seen the other's (Two Leaders); six years of taking turns had hidden it.

steps.title: Last save wins and sorting by time: two easy answers that fail.
steps.text: Last save wins goes in two steps: each laptop sends its whole version of the paragraph, and the server keeps whichever arrives last and sends it to both. The copies match, and one writer's whole edit is gone without a word: his "never" on 2 March, his 5-word sentence on 13 April. Sorting by time also goes in two steps: collect every change, then replay them all in the order typed from the last shared paragraph. Every laptop gets the same order, so the copies match, but each change still carries its raw position: her delete goes first, his insert lands at 40, and both laptops read "She never had the only key." The order was never the problem; the count was. And the times come from two laptops' clocks: Rule 6, never trust the clock on the wall (Never Trust the Clock).

steps.title: Operational transformation: one server shifts the count.
steps.text: This is how Google Docs described its editor in 2010. First, every change goes to one server, saying which version of the document it was made on. Second, the server finds the changes it has already applied since then that this writer had not seen. Third, it transforms the change past each of them: an insert or delete earlier in the text moves its position right or left by that many characters. Fourth, it applies the change, adds it to its history, the revision log, and sends it on, shifted again where the receiving laptop has changes of its own still waiting. Here, N-412 is checked against B-388 and stays at 0, because his insert came after it; B-388 goes to Nomvula's laptop shifted from 40 to 28, just before "locked". What can go wrong: the shifting rules must be right for every pair of change types, and nothing merges without the server, so offline changes wait and are shifted when they arrive.

steps.title: A CRDT: every character gets an id.
steps.text: A CRDT, short for conflict-free replicated data type (Two Leaders), drops positions altogether. First, every character gets a character id no other character has; in the sim, the writer's letter and a count, so the paragraph is N7201 to N7269. Second, an insert is pinned to the id of the character before it: "never " goes after N7240, the space before "locked", in any copy that has N7240. Third, a delete hides ids instead of counting: N-412 hides N7201 to N7212. Each stays as a hidden character, often called a tombstone, so an insert pinned to it still finds its place. Fourth, every laptop applies the same rule, and when two inserts are pinned to one neighbour a fixed tie rule on their ids puts them in the same order everywhere. So the copies converge, ending the same whatever order the changes arrive in, with no server deciding. Yjs and Automerge work this way. What can go wrong: ids and hidden characters cost memory, and the merge never asks whether the result reads well.

steps.title: Figma in the middle, a lock at the edge, and the merge conflict that asks.
steps.text: Figma took a middle way: its data is CRDT-inspired, but its server is the single authority on what the document looks like, which keeps things simpler; it does not try to merge two people typing in the same text box. A chapter lock removes the overlap instead of merging it: no conflicts, but nobody types offline and two writers can't share a chapter. Branches showed the opposite choice: Git stops at a merge conflict and asks a person. Collaborative editors merge without asking, so they must be right by construction, and overlapping edits are still worth a human read.

diagram.aria: The fix replayed for 2 March with ids. At 21:20 my laptop, offline, hides N7201 to N7212. At 21:26 Beckett's laptop sends B-388 to the server: never pinned after N7240. At 23:42 the server sends B-388 to my laptop, and my laptop sends N-412 to the server, which passes it to Beckett's laptop. Both laptops read never before locked.

explain.caption: The fix, replayed for 2 March with ids. My delete hides characters by id, and his insert is pinned after N7240, the space before "locked". Whichever arrives first, both laptops end with "Kaja heard it. The door was never locked. She had the only key."

fix.title: The fix: pin every insert to an id, not a position
fix.text: Move the book to an editor built on a CRDT, such as Yjs or Automerge. Every character carries an id; an insert is recorded as "after this id", a delete as "hide these ids", and every laptop applies the same rule with the same tie rule, so both copies converge on the paragraph both writers meant, offline or not, without asking anyone. If a central server is acceptable, operational transformation through it, as Google Docs does, is the other sound route. Either way, keep the morning read-through, and have the editor mark any paragraph both of you changed while apart, so a person reads the merge.

limits: It merges without asking. If Nomvula deletes a sentence while Beckett inserts a word inside it, his word keeps its place among hidden neighbours and survives on its own, identically on both laptops. A CRDT promises every copy ends the same, not that the result reads as either writer meant.

Ids and hidden characters take memory: every character carries an id, and deleted ones stay as markers. Libraries such as Yjs store runs of typing together to keep this small, but a long book with years of edits still grows.
It means new software on both laptops and the server, and every copy must follow the same rules: one laptop still replaying raw positions would bring the old fault straight back.

head: How changes merge
Good
Bad
rows: Simple; fine while the writers take turns.
Concurrent edits land in the wrong place: "never" 12 characters late, and the laptops differ.
A whole edit vanishes without a word: 1 word on 2 March, 5 on 13 April.
Positions still shift: both laptops read "She never had", and it trusts two laptops' clocks.
Nobody types offline; one writer waits for the other.
Changes land where meant; the server keeps one clear history.
Every merge needs the server; the shifting rules are hard to get right.
Lands where meant on every laptop, offline or not, without asking anyone.
Ids and hidden characters take memory; overlapping edits merge blindly.

explain.seniorTake: When two copies of a text can change apart, the merge rule is the product. A position is only a count, and it means something only in the text it was counted in, so replaying raw positions is correct exactly as long as nobody edits concurrently, which is to say until the first offline flight. Last save wins makes copies match by deleting someone's work; sorting by time makes them match on the same wrong text and trusts clocks besides. The two sound designs both stop treating a count as an address. Operational transformation keeps positions but sends every change through one server that shifts each past the changes it has already applied; it suits an always-online editor with a central service, as Google Docs described in 2010. A CRDT gives every character an id and pins each insert to its neighbour, so any copy can merge any change in any order and still converge; it suits offline-first tools and peer-to-peer sync, at the price of memory for ids and hidden characters. Figma shows you can borrow CRDT ideas and keep a server in charge. Whichever you choose, remember that converging is not the same as meaning well: two edits to one sentence made apart deserve a person's eye, so surface them rather than merging them in silence.

realWorld.title: Google Docs, 2010: the same mistake, and its name
realWorld.text: In "Conflict resolution", 22 September 2010, John Day-Richter shows one editor applying another's delete at its raw position, after two characters the deleting writer never saw had been typed at the start: "He deleted the wrong characters!" Then: "The algorithm that we use to handle these shifts is called operational transformation (OT)."

realWorld.title: Google Docs, 2010: through the server
realWorld.text: The same post closes with the route: "Collaboration in Google Docs consists of sending changes from one editor to the server, and then to the other editors." And: "Each editor transforms incoming changes so that they make sense relative to the local version of the document." The first post of the series describes a change as a position: "That particular change was to insert the letter T at the 10th position in the document."

realWorld.title: Figma, 2019: CRDT-inspired, server in charge
realWorld.text: Evan Wallace explains why Figma did not use OT: "As mentioned earlier, OTs power most collaborative text-based apps such as Google Docs." Then: "Figma isn't using true CRDTs though." Instead, "Since Figma is centralized (our server is the central authority), we can simplify our system". The price for text: "This is why simultaneous editing of the same text value doesn't work in Figma." And offline still works: "Figma lets you go offline for an arbitrary amount of time and continue editing."

realWorld.title: Yjs: a CRDT for shared editing
realWorld.text: Yjs's documentation introduces it as "a high-performance CRDT for building collaborative applications that sync automatically." Its shared types "can be manipulated, fire events when changes happen, and automatically merge without merge conflicts."

realWorld.title: Yjs inside: an id and a neighbour for everything
realWorld.text: Yjs's notes on its internals: "When an item is created, it stores a reference to the IDs of the preceding and succeeding item." Those references settle ties: "Though quite rare in practice, Yjs needs to make sure the list items always resolve to the same order on all peers." And deletes hide rather than remove: "When an item has been deleted by any peer, at any point in history, it is flagged as deleted on the item."

realWorld.title: Automerge: offline, and no central server
realWorld.text: Automerge's documentation: "Each user can independently update the application state on their local device, even while offline, and save the state to local disk." And: "If the state was changed concurrently on different devices, Automerge automatically merges the changes together cleanly, so that everybody ends up in the same state, and no changes are lost."

asked: Design Google Docs: how do two people edit one paragraph at the same time?
OT or CRDT: what is the difference?
Why does last write wins lose data?
interview.answer: I'd start with why the naive design fails. If each edit travels as "insert this at position N", the position was counted in the text its author had, and replaying it on a copy that already holds another concurrent edit puts it in the wrong place; the copies can even end up different. Last write wins avoids the mess by keeping one whole version of the paragraph, which silently drops the other person's edit, and sorting by timestamps gives everyone the same wrong text while trusting clocks. There are two sound designs. Operational transformation sends every edit through one central server, which keeps the history and transforms each incoming edit past the edits it has already applied that the author hadn't seen, shifting its position by whatever was inserted or deleted earlier; clients transform the server's edits past their own pending ones. That's what Google Docs described in 2010; it needs the server and correct transform rules for every pair of operation types. A CRDT gives every character a unique id, records an insert as after a neighbour's id and a delete as a hidden marker, and uses a fixed tie rule, so every copy applies edits in any order and converges without a coordinator; Yjs and Automerge do this, and it suits offline and peer-to-peer sync, at the cost of memory for ids and tombstones. Figma sits between: CRDT-inspired structures with its server as the authority. For a text editor I'd choose OT if we are always online with a central service, a CRDT if offline editing matters, and either way I'd surface overlapping edits for review, because converging isn't the same as matching intent. I'd tell the story of two thriller writers whose app replayed "never" 12 characters late after one of them edited on a plane.

terms.def: The thriller Nomvula, in Johannesburg, and Beckett, in Tucson, are writing: their fourth book together. Its detective is Kaja.
The writers' daily video call at 17:00 in Johannesburg, 08:00 in Tucson, his morning: the newest pages read aloud, each following on their own screen.
Without an internet connection. The writing app keeps a whole copy of the book on each laptop, so a writer can keep working offline, on a plane for instance.

A label no other change has, like a parcel's tracking number: the writer's letter and a count, such as N-412 or B-388. It stops a laptop applying one change twice.
A count of characters from the start of the paragraph, the first being 0. It means something only in the text it was counted in.
One letter, space or punctuation mark. "Rain again. " is 12 characters: 9 letters, 2 spaces and a full stop.
Bringing two copies up to date, in steps: send your new changes, fetch the other side's, then apply them to your own copy.
Making a change that came from another laptop: count to its position in your own copy and insert or delete there.
Edits made without either writer having seen the other's, like Nomvula's on the plane and Beckett's at 21:26. Neither came first in any way the app can see.
The whole text of the paragraph as one laptop has it at one moment.
Keeping whichever version reaches the server last and dropping the other; also called last writer wins. The copies match, and one writer's edit can vanish unseen.
A permission only one writer holds at a time, like a room's single key. A laptop must get it from the server before typing in that chapter, so an offline laptop can't type.
Merging by shifting: every change goes through one server, which moves its position past changes already applied that its writer hadn't seen. Google Docs described it in 2010.
Rewrite a change to fit a text that already has another change: an insert or delete earlier in the text shifts its position by that many characters.
Google Docs' name, in 2010, for the server's history of every change in order. A document is shown by replaying it from the start.
Short for conflict-free replicated data type: a structure whose copies can change apart and always merge to the same result, in any order, without asking anyone (Two Leaders).
In a CRDT, a label only one character has. In the sim, the writer's letter and a count: the paragraph is N7201 to N7269, and "never " is B9301 to B9306.
Record an insert as "after the character with this id" instead of "at this position", so it lands beside the same neighbour in every copy.
A deleted character that a CRDT keeps as an invisible marker, so an insert pinned to it still finds its place. Tombstone is the usual name.
The fixed rule that orders two inserts pinned to the same neighbour, for example by their ids, so every copy puts them the same way round.
End up identical: every copy holds the same text once it has received every change, whatever order they came in.
An open-source CRDT library for shared editing. Every inserted item has an id and remembers the ids of its neighbours; deleted items are flagged, not removed.
An open-source CRDT library for apps that work offline on each device and merge changes from other devices automatically, without a central server.
A design tool that many people edit at once. Its multiplayer system is CRDT-inspired, but its server is the single authority on the document.
Google's online word processor. In 2010 its engineers described merging edits by operational transformation through Google's servers.
An audit report on how a company's systems meet the AICPA's trust services criteria. Its processing integrity criteria (PI1) cover processing that is complete, valid, accurate and timely.

atWork: Look for places where two copies of the same text or record can change while apart: a notes app's offline mode, a mobile app that queues edits on a train, a shared form two people fill in, comments edited on two devices. Read-only access is enough. First, list every feature that syncs edits between devices or users. Second, read what one change carries over the wire: a raw position ("insert at 120"), a whole record that replaces the old one, or ids. Third, ask what happens when two changes made apart meet, and look for a test with one device offline. Raw positions misplace text as soon as two edits overlap; whole-record replacement, last write wins, drops one edit silently. A sync that sends raw positions between devices is a common pattern. Where text is edited by several people, use a library built for it, such as Yjs or Automerge, or route every change through one server that transforms them, and show overlapping edits to a person rather than merging them in silence. Standards: if your company is pursuing SOC 2 and processing integrity is in scope, the PI1 criteria expect system processing to be complete, valid, accurate and timely, and a sync that silently loses or misplaces a user's edit is a gap an auditor could find. Flag for the design: choose the merge model when the data format is designed; retrofitting ids into documents stored as plain positions means migrating every stored document, which is the rework to avoid.

recall.prompt: Your team's notes app works offline on phones and laptops. Each device sends its edits to the others as "insert this text at character 120" or "delete 8 characters at 40". After a user edits a note on a phone in a tunnel while a colleague edits it on a laptop, words appear in the middle of other words, and the two devices show different notes. What is happening, and what would you change?

keyIdeas.idea: A position is counted in the text it was made on; the other device's concurrent edit shifted that text, so replaying the raw number lands in the wrong place
Give every character a unique id and pin inserts to a neighbour's id, so every device merges the same way: a CRDT such as Yjs or Automerge
Or send every edit through one server that transforms each position past edits it has already applied: operational transformation

recall.model: Each edit's position was counted in the text on the device that made it. While the phone was in the tunnel, the laptop's edit shifted that text, so when the phone's edit was replayed at its raw number it landed in the wrong place, inside other words; and because each device replayed the other's edit on a different text, the two ended with different notes. The edits were concurrent, and raw positions can't survive that. I'd stop sending raw positions. Either give every character a unique id and pin each insert to its neighbour's id, so every device applies the same edits the same way in any order and they converge, a CRDT such as Yjs or Automerge; or send every edit through one server that transforms each position past the edits it has already applied, operational transformation, as Google Docs does. Either way I'd add a test with one device offline.

recall.prompt: In the sim, on 2 March with Nomvula's laptop offline and no lock, which merge method leaves both laptops matching, but with "never" before "had"?
options: Sort by the time each change was typed
Shifting every change past earlier ones at the server
recall.why: Sorting puts her delete (21:20) before his insert (21:26) and replays both at their raw positions on both laptops, so both read "She never had the only key": they match, 12 characters late. Replaying positions leaves the laptops different; last save wins drops "never"; operational transformation shifts it from 40 to 28, where he meant.

recall.prompt: On 2 March, why did Beckett's copy come out right while Nomvula's did not?
options: His laptop's clock was more accurate than hers
Her delete sat before his insert, so replaying it didn't move his word; his insert sat after her delete, so replaying it at 40 in her shorter copy did
The server corrected his copy but could not reach hers
His version reached the server last, so it won
recall.why: A change further along a paragraph never moves the count to an earlier spot. Her delete at position 0 came before "never", so replayed on his copy it simply removed "Rain again. ". His insert came after her cut, so his count of 40 meant 12 characters later in her copy. No clock or saving rule was involved: the app only replayed positions.

recall.prompt: In an interview you're asked to design Google Docs: two people type in one paragraph at the same moment. How do you combine their work, and how do the two well-known designs differ?

keyIdeas.idea: Raw positions break, because a position only means something in the text it was counted in
Operational transformation: a central server orders edits and transforms each one past edits it has already applied
A CRDT gives every character a unique id, pins inserts to neighbours and converges in any order without a coordinator, at a memory cost

recall.model: Sending edits as raw positions fails, because a position is counted in the text its author had; replay it on a copy that already has someone else's concurrent edit and it lands in the wrong place. One sound design is operational transformation: every edit goes to one central server, which keeps a revision log and transforms each incoming edit past the edits it has already applied that the author hadn't seen, shifting its position; Google Docs described this in 2010. The other is a CRDT: every character gets a unique id, an insert is pinned to its neighbour's id, deletes become tombstones, and a fixed tie rule means every copy can apply edits in any order and still converge with no coordinator, as Yjs and Automerge do; the cost is memory for ids and tombstones. I'd pick OT for an always-online product with a central service and a CRDT where offline editing matters, and flag overlapping edits for a person either way.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 4 months later. The new app has merged every flight since March, the April copy-edits included, and The Only Key comes out in August. On Tuesday 22 June I flew to Cape Town for a radio interview about it, offline from 19:40 to 22:55. At 20:30, in the air, I cut a whole sentence from chapter 4 of our fifth book: "The lift was out of order. ", 27 characters, positions 13 to 39 of "Kaja waited. The lift was out of order. Then she took the stairs." At 20:36 my time, 11:36 his, Beckett, online, typed "still " just before "out". At Wednesday's read-through both laptops showed exactly the same paragraph, as the app promises: "Kaja waited. still Then she took the stairs." Neither of us typed "still" there on purpose. Beckett says the app is broken again.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. Why did "still" survive on both laptops, is the app broken, and what should they change?

keyIdeas.idea: His insert was pinned to a character she deleted; deleted characters stay as hidden markers, so his word kept its place among them and survived alone
Not broken: a CRDT guarantees every copy ends the same, not that the result reads as either writer meant
Flag edits made apart that overlap the same sentence for a person to accept or reject at the read-through

coldCase.model: Beckett's "still " was pinned to the id of the character before it, the space after "was", inside the sentence Nomvula cut. Her delete didn't remove those characters; it turned them into hidden markers, tombstones, so his insert kept its place among them and, with its neighbours hidden, survived on its own. Both laptops applied the same changes by the same rule, so both ended the same. The app is not broken: it is working as designed. A CRDT guarantees that every copy will converge, not that the result reads the way either writer meant; it merges without asking, so it can't know that a word added to a deleted sentence should go with it. Keep the CRDT and add a person back in for overlaps: have the app mark any sentence that both of them changed while apart and show both versions as a suggestion to accept or reject, or highlight it for review at the read-through, so a person reads a merge like this before it is trusted.
